title: The recital
hookLine: at the first council Mahakassapa asks and Ananda answers: where each discourse was spoken, and to whom (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
tomorrow: The couple who didn't want to marry

cards: One elder asks. One elder answers. The teacher who spoke these words is gone, and a room full of elders at Rajagaha has one job: make sure what he said doesn't drift away.
So the Vinaya describes something like a very calm exam. Mahakassapa, presiding, asks. Ananda answers.
Everyone else listens closely, because once the answers are agreed, this is the teaching they will carry. It all rests on one man's memory, and on a room willing to check it.

teach.h: WHERE WAS IT SPOKEN? TO WHOM?
teach.b: First, the questions. They're about place and people before doctrine. In the Vinaya's account Kassapa asks: where was the discourse called the Net of Brahma spoken?
Ananda answers: on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at the king's rest house in Ambalatthika. And about whom? A wanderer named Suppiya and a young brahmin, his pupil.
Then the next discourse, and the next, through the collections. Second, why place and people.
A teaching remembered with its setting is harder to bend.
If you know who was standing there and what they asked, you know what the answer was answering. It may be part of why the discourses begin with a town, a grove, a person. Third, an honest gap.
Ananda also reports that near the end the Buddha told him the community could drop the lesser and minor rules after he was gone. Which ones, the elders ask. And Ananda has to say he didn't ask.
They talk it over, Kassapa proposes keeping every rule as it was, and the elders agree. A good memory also remembers what it never got.
Fourth, the room. Tradition says the elders chanted it back together, and from then on the teaching lived in voices: groups of monks reciting it aloud, generation after generation.
One man remembered. A whole room made sure the memory held.

how: Monks and nuns in Theravada communities still learn discourses and verses by heart and chant them together, and the recitation of texts is a regular part of monastery life.

o: a monk's private chanting each morning

p: spoken at the rest house in Ambalatthika

s: the council wrote the teaching down in books
in the Vinaya's account it is recited and chanted back; the teaching lived in voices.

the setting comes first, so the teaching stays tied to what it was answering.

games.q: the elders ask which minor rules the Buddha said could be dropped. Ananda never asked. what does the council do?
o: drop the rules that seem minor to them.
keep every rule as it was.
let each monk decide for himself.
games.why: Kassapa proposes keeping all of them, and the council agrees: better not to guess at what the teacher meant.

practice: Recite one verse by heart: a line from any tradition you love, or this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."

Say it slowly three or four times, out loud if you can, then close your eyes and say it without looking. Where you stumble, look once and try again, and when it holds, let it go quiet and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The recital. At the first council Kassapa asks where each discourse was spoken and to whom, and Ananda answers from memory. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali bahussuta, one who has heard much: the discourses name Ananda foremost among the learned in this sense (AN 1.14).

carryVoice: Your line: he remembered. A setting keeps the meaning from bending. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.
